solution.concept_anchor: J&K LC abolition 2019 vs Andhra Pradesh LC abolition 2020
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) reverses the order of the J&K reorganisation and the Andhra Pradesh abolition, which students who remember 'both happened around 2019–2020' without precise dating will frequently choose.
elimination_logic: Fix anchor 1: Bihar's LC was abolished in 1969 — earliest event; comes first.
Fix anchor 2: J&K Reorganisation Act 2019 abolished the J&K Legislative Council — second in sequence.
Fix anchor 3: Andhra Pradesh's Legislative Council was abolished in 2020 — latest event.
Correct order: Bihar abolition (1969) → J&K reorganisation and LC abolition (2019) → Andhra Pradesh LC abolition (2020) — option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap targets the J&K (2019) and Andhra Pradesh (2020) events, which occurred in consecutive years and are frequently confused. Students who know 'both happened recently' but haven't fixed the precise years will reverse them. The question anchors the sequence with Bihar (1969) — a distant event — ensuring that the subtle trap is between positions 2 and 3, not between 1 and the others.
solution.final_explanation:
Three significant LC abolition events in Indian history are tested here.

1. Bihar (1969): Bihar's Legislative Council was abolished in 1969 through the Article 169 route — making it the earliest state to abolish its LC. (Bihar later recreated its LC in 2004.)
2. Jammu & Kashmir (2019): The J&K Reorganisation Act 2019 bifurcated J&K into two UTs — J&K (with legislature) and Ladakh (without legislature). The J&K LC was abolished as part of this reorganisation. This was done through ordinary parliamentary legislation, not Article 169.
3. Andhra Pradesh (2020): The AP Legislative Assembly passed a resolution in 2019, and Parliament enacted the necessary law — AP's LC was formally abolished in 2020.

Why wrong options fail: Option (a) places J&K after AP — incorrect. Option (b) reverses J&K and AP. Option (d) misplaces Bihar.

Value Addition:
• Bihar is the only state to have abolished and then recreated its LC — abolished 1969, recreated 2004.
• J&K's LC abolition was through reorganisation legislation, not Article 169 — a nuanced distinction.
• As of 2024, five states retain their LCs: UP, Bihar (recreated), Maharashtra, Karnataka, Telangana.

solution.concept_anchor: LC powers over ordinary vs Money Bills — comparative limits

statement_analysis.statement: The Legislative Council can delay a Money Bill for a maximum period of fourteen days, after which the bill is deemed to have been passed by both Houses in the form approved by the Legislative Assembly.
statement_analysis.reason: This precisely reflects Article 198 — the LC's power on Money Bills is limited to a 14-day delay. After 14 days, the bill is deemed passed whether or not the LC has acted.

statement_analysis.statement: The Legislative Council can delay an ordinary bill for a maximum of six months in total across two rounds of detention before the Legislative Assembly's version prevails.
statement_analysis.reason: The total maximum delay is 4 months — 3 months on the first detention and 1 month on the second detention under Article 197. The 6-month figure is the inter-session gap rule under Article 174, not the LC's delay power.

statement_analysis.statement: The Legislative Council may suggest amendments to a Money Bill but the Legislative Assembly is not constitutionally obligated to accept any of those suggestions.
statement_analysis.reason: Under Articles 198/207, the LC may return a Money Bill with recommendations, but the LA has absolute discretion to accept or reject them — the LA's version is final.

solution.strong_distractor: c — 2 and 3 only is a strong distractor because students who correctly identify Statement 2 as incorrect may also doubt Statement 3, assuming that the LC's power to 'suggest' implies some obligation on the LA to consider the suggestions formally — conflating procedure with obligation.
elimination_logic: Test Statement 1: LC delay on Money Bill — 14 days, then deemed passed — Article 198; Statement 1 is correct (NOT incorrect).
Test Statement 2: Total LC delay on ordinary bills = 3 + 1 = 4 months, NOT 6 months; Statement 2 IS incorrect.
Test Statement 3: LC suggestions on Money Bills are not binding on LA — Article 198 makes LA's will absolute; Statement 3 is correct (NOT incorrect).
Only Statement 2 is incorrect — correct option is (b): 2 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is a partial-truth: it correctly identifies that the LC has two rounds of detention but incorrectly states the total as 6 months. The 6-month figure is real but belongs to a different provision — the inter-session gap under Article 174. Students who know 'there is a 6-month rule somewhere in state legislature provisions' will conflate the two, accepting Statement 2 as correct and therefore not marking it as incorrect.
solution.final_explanation:
Understanding the LC's delay powers requires distinguishing between the two categories of bills and the precise time periods applicable to each.

• Statement 1 — Correct (not incorrect): 14-day delay on Money Bills — Article 198; deemed passed if LC fails to act within 14 days.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The total LC delay on ordinary bills is 4 months (3 + 1), not 6 months. Six months is the maximum inter-session gap under Article 174 — a completely different provision.
• Statement 3 — Correct (not incorrect): LC suggestions on Money Bills are non-binding on the LA. The LA may accept none, some, or all of them — its will is constitutionally absolute on Money Bills.

Only Statement 2 is NOT correct.

Value Addition:
• LC on Money Bills: 14 days delay only; suggestions non-binding.
• LC on Ordinary Bills: 3 months (first) + 1 month (second) = 4 months maximum delay.
• No joint sitting for state legislature deadlocks — Article 197 time-lapse override instead.

solution.concept_anchor: Speaker presiding during removal — Deputy presides; Speaker votes in first instance

statement_analysis.statement: When a resolution for the removal of the Speaker of the Legislative Assembly is being considered, the Deputy Speaker presides over that sitting.
statement_analysis.reason: During the consideration of a resolution for the Speaker's removal, the Speaker does not preside — the Deputy Speaker takes the chair. This is a constitutional safeguard against conflict of interest.

statement_analysis.statement: When a resolution for the removal of the Speaker is being considered, the Speaker is debarred from presiding but also from speaking or voting on the resolution.
statement_analysis.reason: While the Speaker cannot preside during the removal resolution, the Speaker retains the right to speak and vote as a member in the first instance (not just a casting vote). The restriction is only on presiding — not on participation as a member.

statement_analysis.statement: The Speaker of the Legislative Assembly does not vacate office merely because the Assembly has been dissolved — the Speaker continues until the first sitting of the newly constituted Assembly.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 179 expressly provides that the Speaker continues in office even after the dissolution of the Assembly until the first sitting of the next Assembly — ensuring institutional continuity.

statement_analysis.statement: The casting vote of the Speaker is exercised in all circumstances where the Speaker wishes to express a preference, not merely in cases of equality of votes.
statement_analysis.reason: The Speaker's casting vote is exercised only in cases of equality of votes — it is a tie-breaking mechanism, not a preference-expressing tool. The Speaker does not ordinarily vote.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Only two is a strong distractor because students who correctly identify Statement 2 as incorrect may be uncertain about Statement 4, and those who know Statement 4 is incorrect may not precisely recall the nuance in Statement 2 — leading them to count only one incorrect statement instead of two.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: Deputy Speaker presides during Speaker removal resolution — constitutionally correct; Statement 1 is correct.
Verify Statement 2: Speaker cannot preside but CAN speak and vote in first instance — Statement 2's claim of total debarment from speaking/voting is incorrect.
Verify Statement 3: Speaker continues after dissolution until new Assembly's first sitting — Article 179; Statement 3 is correct.
Verify Statement 4: Casting vote is only in case of equality of votes, not general preference — Statement 4 is incorrect.
Statements 1 and 3 correct; Statements 2 and 4 incorrect — 2 statements correct out of 4 — correct option is (b): Only two.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is a subtle partial-truth trap. Students know 'the Speaker cannot preside during the removal resolution' — this is correct. But the statement extends this to 'also from speaking or voting,' which is false. The Speaker retains full membership rights (speaking, voting in first instance) — only the presiding function is transferred to the Deputy Speaker. Students who conflate 'cannot preside' with 'cannot participate at all' will accept Statement 2 as correct, leading to an overcount.
solution.final_explanation:
These four statements test precise knowledge of the Speaker's powers, limitations, and continuity of office.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Deputy Speaker presides when the removal resolution against the Speaker is under consideration — a constitutional safeguard.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The Speaker cannot preside during their own removal resolution, but retains the right to speak and vote as a member in the first instance. The restriction is on presiding only.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Article 179 ensures the Speaker continues in office after dissolution until the new Assembly's first sitting — a key continuity provision.
• Statement 4 — Incorrect: The casting vote is strictly a tie-breaking mechanism exercised only when votes are equal — not a general preference-expressing vote. The Speaker does not ordinarily vote.

Only 2 statements are correct.

Value Addition:
• Speaker during removal: cannot preside, but CAN speak and vote (unlike normal casting-vote-only rule).
• Article 179: Speaker vacates if ceases to be a member — but NOT merely because of dissolution.
• Anti-defection: Speaker is the sole authority under Tenth Schedule — quasi-judicial function.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 194 — freedom of speech in state legislature and civil arrest protection
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because both A and R are true, and students may question whether the civil arrest protection (R) is the actual reason why no court proceedings lie (A) — they are related but A refers to speech/vote in the House, while R refers to arrest during sessions.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. Article 194(1) grants absolute freedom of speech in the state legislature; Article 194(2) says no member shall be liable to any proceedings in any court for anything said or voted in the legislature.
Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — Yes. Article 194(3) grants members protection from civil arrest during the session, and 40 days before and after the session.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — No. A is about immunity from court proceedings for speech/votes in the House — this flows from Article 194(1) and (2). R is about protection from civil arrest — a separate privilege under Article 194(3). R does not cause or explain A — they are parallel privileges under the same article but causally independent.
Both A and R are correct but R does not explain A — correct option is (b).
solution.final_explanation:
Article 194 creates a cluster of legislative privileges for state legislature members — these privileges are parallel to those of Parliament under Article 105 but apply specifically to state legislatures.

Assertion (A): Correct. Article 194(2) provides that no member of a state legislature shall be liable to any proceedings in any court in respect of anything said or any vote given in the legislature. This is an absolute protection for legislative speech and votes.

Reason (R): Correct. Article 194(3) protects members from civil arrest during the session period and for 40 days before and after the session. Criminal arrest is not covered by this protection.

Causal relationship: A and R are parallel privileges from Article 194 — both are true, but they protect different things. A protects members from court action for their legislative speech/votes; R protects members from civil arrest during sessions. R does not explain why A exists — both flow independently from the privilege doctrine. Therefore, R is not the correct explanation of A.

Value Addition:
• Article 194 mirrors Article 105 — same structure, applicable to state legislatures.
• MSM Sharma v. Sri Krishna Sinha (1959): Legislative privilege can override Article 19(1)(a) in certain contexts.
• State legislatures cannot claim privileges beyond Parliament's privileges as they existed in 1950 (until codified by law).

solution.concept_anchor: Article 66 — Vice Presidential election excludes state legislatures entirely
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because students who know 'elected MLAs participate in Presidential election' extend this logic to the Vice Presidential election, assuming state legislators have some role in electing both the President and Vice President.
elimination_logic: Identify the applicable rule: Article 66 governs the Vice Presidential election — it is elected by members of both Houses of Parliament in a joint meeting.
Eliminate (a): Only elected MLAs of state legislatures have a role in Presidential elections (Article 54) — but none of them participate in the Vice Presidential election.
Eliminate (b): State legislators (whether LA or LC, elected or nominated) have zero role in the Vice Presidential election under Article 66.
Eliminate (c): Only elected members of state LAs participate in Presidential election — LC members are excluded from even the Presidential electoral college, let alone the VP election.
Confirm (d): The Vice Presidential election is conducted entirely among members of both Houses of Parliament — the state legislature members have no role at all in the Vice Presidential election.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: This question exploits the natural extension of the Presidential election rule to the Vice Presidential election. Students who know state legislators participate in the Presidential election often assume some state-level input exists for the Vice Presidential election too. The Vice Presidential election is a parliamentary affair only — state legislators have zero involvement. The trap also operates in reverse: students who know LC members are excluded from the Presidential election may assume LC members are similarly excluded from the VP election for the same reason — which is partially true but for the wrong reason (the right reason is that no state legislators participate at all).
solution.final_explanation:
The electoral college provisions for the President and Vice President are structured very differently under Articles 54–66.

Scenario analysis: The members of both the LA and LC of a state have NO role whatsoever in the election of the Vice President. Article 66 provides that the Vice President shall be elected by the members of an electoral college consisting of members of both Houses of Parliament (Lok Sabha + Rajya Sabha) in a joint meeting.

• Option (a): Incorrect. Elected MLAs participate in the Presidential election (Article 54) but have zero role in the Vice Presidential election.
• Option (b): Incorrect. Neither LA nor LC members (elected or nominated) participate in the Vice Presidential election.
• Option (c): Incorrect. Even elected MLAs — who participate in Presidential election — have no role in the VP election.
• Option (d): Correct. The VP election is exclusively for Parliament members (both Houses). State legislators are completely excluded.

Value Addition:
• Presidential electoral college: elected MLAs + elected MPs (both Houses).
• Vice Presidential electoral college: all members of both Houses of Parliament (elected AND nominated).
• Nominated Rajya Sabha members CAN vote in the Vice Presidential election — unlike the Presidential election where nominated members are excluded.

solution.concept_anchor: DC Wadhwa case — re-promulgation of ordinances condemned

statement_analysis.statement: An ordinance promulgated by the Governor under Article 213 has the same force and effect as an Act of the state legislature, provided it is within the Governor's legislative competence.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 213(2) expressly provides that an ordinance promulgated by the Governor shall have the same force and effect as an Act of the state legislature — subject to the same constitutional limitations on state legislative power.

statement_analysis.statement: The Governor may promulgate an ordinance even when the state legislature is in session, provided the ordinance relates to an urgent matter of national security.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 213 permits ordinance promulgation only when the state legislature (or one House in bicameral states) is not in session. There is no exception allowing ordinances during a session — not even for urgent matters.

statement_analysis.statement: The Supreme Court has condemned the practice of re-promulgating ordinances by state Governors, holding it to be a fraud on the Constitution.
statement_analysis.reason: In DC Wadhwa v. State of Bihar (1987), the Supreme Court condemned re-promulgation of ordinances as a fraud on the Constitution and held that the executive cannot bypass the legislature by repeatedly re-issuing ordinances without legislative approval.

solution.strong_distractor: d — 1, 2 and 3 is a strong distractor because Statement 2 sounds constitutionally reasonable — students may assume that national security urgency creates an implied exception to the 'not in session' requirement for ordinances.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: Ordinances have same force as state legislation — Article 213(2); Statement 1 is correct.
Verify Statement 2: Ordinances can only be promulgated when legislature is NOT in session — no exception for urgency during a session; Statement 2 is incorrect.
Verify Statement 3: DC Wadhwa (1987) condemned re-promulgation as fraud on Constitution — applies to Governors; Statement 3 is correct.
Statements 1 and 3 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — correct option is (c): 1 and 3 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits the assumption that 'national security urgency' overrides procedural requirements for ordinances. The Constitution does not provide such an exception — the requirement that the legislature must not be in session is absolute. If the legislature is in session, the appropriate mechanism is to introduce an emergency bill, not an ordinance. Students who know ordinances are 'for urgent situations' may accept Statement 2 without recalling the 'not in session' condition.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 213 governs the Governor's ordinance-making power — a significant executive tool that substitutes for legislation during legislative recesses.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Article 213(2) gives ordinances the same force as state legislation. They can amend, repeal, or create law within the state's legislative competence.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Ordinances can only be promulgated when the legislature is not in session (or when one House is not in session in a bicameral state). There is no 'national security' exception that permits ordinances during a session — the Constitution's text is unambiguous.
• Statement 3 — Correct: DC Wadhwa v. State of Bihar (1987) is a landmark judgment specifically condemning the Bihar Governor's practice of re-promulgating ordinances repeatedly without seeking legislative approval. The Court held this to be a 'fraud on the Constitution' — the doctrine applies to all state Governors.

Value Addition:
• RC Cooper case principle: Ordinance power is co-extensive with legislative power — same subjects, same limitations.
• Governor ordinance lapses if: (i) legislature disapproves it, (ii) it is withdrawn, (iii) not laid before legislature, or (iv) 6 weeks after reassembly pass without approval.
• DC Wadhwa 1987 condemned 'ordinance raj' — same principle applied by SC to Governors.

solution.concept_anchor: LC retirement schedule governed by Parliament-made law, not President's notification
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because students familiar with the Rajya Sabha's retirement process — where the President determines the retirement schedule — assume the same mechanism applies to state Legislative Councils.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): For Rajya Sabha, the President determines retirement batches — but for state LCs, it is Parliament-made law, not the President, that governs retirement schedules.
Eliminate (c): The Governor does not notify LC retirement schedules — this function is governed by Parliament-made law under Article 172.
Eliminate (d): The Chief Minister has no role in determining LC members' retirement schedules — this is a statutory/legal mechanism, not a political one.
Confirm (b): LC retirement schedules are governed by Parliament-made law — a notable distinction from the Rajya Sabha, where the President's notification is the mechanism.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap conflates the Rajya Sabha's retirement mechanism (Presidential notification) with the LC's retirement mechanism (Parliament-made law). Both are permanent Houses with 6-year terms and 1/3 retirement every 2 years — the structure is identical. But the procedural mechanism for determining which members retire in which batch differs. Students who know the Rajya Sabha's Presidential notification mechanism apply it to LCs, choosing option (a). The correct answer requires knowing this specific difference.
solution.final_explanation:
Both the Rajya Sabha and state Legislative Councils are permanent Houses with 6-year terms and 1/3 retirement every 2 years. However, the mechanism governing which members retire in which batch differs.

• Option (a): Incorrect. For the Rajya Sabha, the President issues notifications specifying retirement batches. This mechanism does NOT apply to Legislative Councils.
• Option (b): Correct. For state Legislative Councils, the retirement schedule is determined by Parliament-made law under Article 172. The allocation of members to retirement batches is a statutory matter, not a Presidential or Gubernatorial discretionary act.
• Option (c): Incorrect. The Governor has no role in determining LC retirement schedules — the Governor's powers relate to summoning, prorogation, and dissolution of the LA, not LC retirement.
• Option (d): Incorrect. The Chief Minister has no role in LC members' retirement scheduling — this is a statutory/legal framework question.

Value Addition:
• Rajya Sabha retirements: governed by Article 83 + Presidential notifications.
• LC retirements: governed by Article 172 + Parliament-made law.
• Both Houses: 6-year term, 1/3 retire every 2 years — structure identical; mechanism differs.
• Governor can extend LC members' terms during national emergency under Article 172(1) proviso.

solution.concept_anchor: Kihoto Hollohan — judicial review after Speaker's decision, not during

statement_analysis.statement: Under the Tenth Schedule, the decision of the Speaker of the Legislative Assembly or the Chairman of the Legislative Council on a disqualification petition is subject to judicial review, but only after the presiding officer has made the decision — courts cannot intervene during the pendency of proceedings before the Speaker or Chairman.
statement_analysis.reason: Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992) precisely held this: the Speaker/Chairman's decision is quasi-judicial and subject to judicial review, but courts will not intervene mid-proceedings — review is available only after the decision is made.

statement_analysis.statement: The Tenth Schedule requires that when a disqualification petition is filed against a member, the Speaker or Chairman must refer the matter to the Election Commission of India for a final determination.
statement_analysis.reason: The Tenth Schedule vests the decision-making authority exclusively in the Speaker (for LA members) and the Chairman (for LC members) — there is no provision for referral to the Election Commission. The ECI's role in disqualification is under Article 103 (for Parliament members under Article 102(1)), not under the Tenth Schedule.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because students who correctly identify Statement 1 as true often accept Statement 2 based on a vague recollection that the Election Commission has some role in disqualification matters — conflating Article 103 (ECI role for MPs) with Tenth Schedule (Speaker/Chairman role for defection).
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: Kihoto Hollohan (1992) — judicial review available only after Speaker's decision, not during proceedings; Statement 1 is correct.

Verify Statement 2: Tenth Schedule gives decision-making power to Speaker/Chairman — no referral to ECI; ECI's role is in Article 103/191 disqualifications, not anti-defection; Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — correct option is (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits a conflation between two different disqualification mechanisms. The Election Commission of India has a role in disqualifications under Articles 103 and 191 (office of profit, etc.) — the President/Governor decides on the ECI's opinion. But the Tenth Schedule creates an entirely separate mechanism: the Speaker/Chairman decides, not the ECI. Students who know 'ECI has a role in legislative disqualifications' apply this knowledge incorrectly to the Tenth Schedule context.
solution.final_explanation:
The Tenth Schedule creates a distinct anti-defection disqualification mechanism separate from other disqualification provisions.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Kihoto Hollohan judgment (1992) is precise on this point — the Speaker/Chairman's decision under the Tenth Schedule is quasi-judicial. Courts can review it on grounds of malice, perversity, or constitutional violation — but only after the decision. Courts will not interdict the Speaker/Chairman during pending proceedings.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: There is no referral to the Election Commission under the Tenth Schedule. The Speaker decides for LA members; the Chairman decides for LC members. The ECI's role in disqualifications (Article 103/191) applies to office of profit and other disqualifications — not to anti-defection cases.

Value Addition:
• Article 102/191 disqualifications (office of profit, etc.): President/Governor decides on ECI's opinion.
• Tenth Schedule disqualification (defection): Speaker (LA) or Chairman (LC) decides — no ECI involvement.
• Kihoto Hollohan upheld Tenth Schedule constitutionality — it was challenged as violating parliamentary democracy.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 200 Governor options — cannot withhold assent second time for ordinary bills

statement_analysis.statement: When a Governor withholds assent to a non-Money Bill and returns it for reconsideration, the Governor is constitutionally obligated to give assent if the legislature passes the bill again — whether or not the legislature makes any amendments.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 200 uses the word 'shall' — if the legislature reconsiders and returns the bill (with or without amendment), the Governor shall give assent. The Governor's discretion is extinguished after the first return for reconsideration.

statement_analysis.statement: A Governor may reserve a non-Money Bill for Presidential consideration even after the state legislature has reconsidered the bill following the Governor's initial return.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 200 provides that after the legislature reconsidering and returning the bill, the Governor 'shall' give assent — the reservation option applies at first presentation, not after reconsideration. Reserving after reconsideration would circumvent the mandatory 'shall' assent obligation.

statement_analysis.statement: For bills reserved for Presidential consideration under Article 201, the President is not bound to give assent even if the state legislature reconsidering the bill passes it a second time.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 201 creates an asymmetry — unlike the Governor's mandatory 'shall' after reconsideration, the President retains full discretion on reserved bills even after the state legislature's reconsideration.

solution.strong_distractor: c — 2 and 3 only is a strong distractor because students who correctly identify Statement 2 as incorrect may second-guess Statement 3 — incorrectly assuming the same mandatory 'shall' rule from Article 200 (Governor) extends to the President under Article 201.
elimination_logic: Test Statement 1: Governor must assent after reconsideration (Article 200 'shall') — Statement 1 is correct (NOT incorrect).
Test Statement 2: Governor cannot reserve after reconsideration — the 'shall' assent obligation under Article 200 kicks in; Statement 2 IS incorrect.
Test Statement 3: President not bound after Article 201 reconsideration — asymmetry with Article 200 is correct; Statement 3 is correct (NOT incorrect).
Only Statement 2 is NOT correct — correct option is (a): 2 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is a partial-truth: reservation for Presidential consideration IS a valid Governor option — but only at first presentation. The trap is the 'after reconsideration' qualifier. Once the legislature reconsidered and returned the bill, the Governor's 'shall' obligation under Article 200 is triggered — the Governor cannot at this stage switch to the reservation route. Students who know 'reservation is an option for Governors' accept Statement 2 without noting the timing restriction.
solution.final_explanation:
Articles 200 and 201 create a deliberate asymmetry between the Governor's and President's powers over state legislation.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Article 200's mandatory 'shall' is absolute after reconsideration — the Governor must assent regardless of amendments made or not made by the legislature. (Not incorrect)
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: After the legislature reconsidering and returning the bill, the Governor must assent under Article 200. The reservation option (Article 200 third option) applies at first presentation — not as an escape route after the mandatory reassent stage is reached. Using reservation at this stage would defeat the mandatory 'shall.'
• Statement 3 — Correct: Article 201 does not bind the President after state reconsideration — unlike Article 200's mandatory 'shall' for Governors. The President's discretion persists. (Not incorrect)

Value Addition:
• SC in State of Punjab v. Principal Secretary to Governor (2023): Governor cannot create 'pocket veto' by indefinitely sitting on bills — Article 200's 'shall' is enforceable.
• Article 200 Governor options at first presentation: assent / withhold / return / reserve.
• After reconsideration: only 'assent' remains — other options are exhausted.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 252 — state request triggers Parliament to legislate on State List
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because students who know 'Rajya Sabha can pass a resolution to allow Parliament to legislate on State List' (Article 249) apply this to Article 252, confusing the two separate mechanisms.
elimination_logic: Identify what Article 252 requires: two or more state legislatures must pass resolutions requesting Parliament to legislate on a State List subject.
Eliminate (a): Rajya Sabha 2/3 resolution → Article 249 (national interest) — not Article 252.
Eliminate (b): Lok Sabha simple majority → not a mechanism in Articles 249 or 252; plausible-fabrication.
Eliminate (d): President's proclamation of emergency → triggers Article 250 (Parliament can legislate on State List during emergency) — not Article 252.
Confirm (c): Two or more state legislatures passing resolutions requesting Parliament to legislate — this is precisely Article 252's mechanism.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap between Articles 249 and 252 is one of the most productive UPSC traps in legislative competence questions. Both allow Parliament to legislate on the State List — but the triggers are entirely different. Article 249 is Rajya Sabha-initiated; Article 252 is state legislature-initiated. Students who know 'a special resolution somewhere allows Parliament to enter the State List' will associate this with the Rajya Sabha and choose option (a). Precise article-to-trigger mapping is the required knowledge.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 252 is one of several provisions allowing Parliament to legislate on State List subjects under specific conditions. The trigger mechanism is unique — it comes from the states themselves.

• Option (a): Incorrect. A Rajya Sabha 2/3 resolution (national interest) is Article 249's mechanism — not Article 252's.
• Option (b): Incorrect. There is no provision for a Lok Sabha simple majority to trigger Parliament's legislative power over State List subjects — this is a plausible fabrication.
• Option (c): Correct. Under Article 252, if two or more state legislatures pass resolutions requesting Parliament to legislate on a State List subject, Parliament is empowered to do so. Other states can later adopt the law by resolution.
• Option (d): Incorrect. A Presidential proclamation of national emergency triggers Article 250 — Parliament may legislate on State List during emergency. This is a different provision from Article 252.

Value Addition:
• Article 249: Rajya Sabha 2/3 majority → national interest → Parliament legislates on State List for 1 year (renewable).
• Article 252: 2+ state legislature resolutions → Parliament legislates → other states may adopt by resolution.
• Article 253: International treaty obligations → Parliament can legislate on State List without state consent.
• Article 250: National emergency → Parliament has full power over State List.

Under Article 252 of the Constitution, Parliament becomes empowered to legislate with respect to a matter in the State List when ________.

(a) The Rajya Sabha passes a resolution by not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting declaring it expedient in the national interest for Parliament to do so
(b) The Lok Sabha passes a resolution by a simple majority requesting Parliament to assume legislative competence over the subject
(c) Two or more state legislatures pass resolutions requesting Parliament to enact a law regulating that matter
(d) The President issues a proclamation declaring a national emergency, thereby conferring temporary legislative competence on Parliament over the State List
